strengths: Combining label propagation or label spreading with classifier-based Bayesian optimization is a sensible, potentially useful contribution, particularly when unlabeled candidate pools are readily available. The manuscript clearly relates this combination to BORE, LFBO, and established semi-supervised learning methods.

The evaluation covers continuous and finite-pool synthetic optimization, four tabular benchmarks, three NATS-Bench datasets, and an image-search task. Comparisons include GP-EI, GP-UCB, and multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers over 10 repetitions. The reported curves show promising improvements, including faster progress on NATS-Bench.

The supplementary ablations investigate bandwidth, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. The comparison without unlabeled data in Figure s.5 provides useful evidence that adding unlabeled points can improve optimization on the tested functions.
weaknesses: The main theoretical conclusion is unsupported. Section 4.3 invokes existence and minimax classification-error results, but does not show that the proposed label-propagation/spreading estimator satisfies those bounds. Nor does it connect classification risk to acquisition maximization or optimization regret. The claim following Eq. (8) that the inductive model is better than or equivalent to supervised alternatives therefore does not follow. Furthermore, 100 unlabeled points in runs reaching 500 evaluations do not match the invoked regime of substantially more unlabeled than labeled data.

Sampling from truncated Gaussians does not establish Assumption 4.1. The cluster assumption concerns alignment between input density and objective-derived labels; Gaussian components centered on observed points can connect regions with different labels. Adaptive sampling and changing quantile thresholds further complicate this alignment. The asserted reduction in the margin and expansion of the favorable decision region are also not established. These gaps undermine the proposed explanation for why the method works.

The overconfidence diagnosis is insufficiently validated. Section 3.1 defines it through the size of the high-probability region, but a small region need not be erroneous, and enlarging that region need not improve exploration. The Branin visualizations and regret ablations do not isolate this mechanism. Quantitative measurements of promising-region coverage, together with supervised smoothing or explicit-exploration baselines and matched randomized tie-breaking, would help distinguish the proposed explanation from simpler alternatives.

Important experimental details remain unspecified, including bandwidth and clamping settings for the main comparisons, propagation stopping parameters, input scaling and categorical encoding, application-pool subset sizes, and acquisition maximization over discrete pools. Figure s.4 shows substantial bandwidth sensitivity, making the missing settings and selection protocol consequential. The promised future code release does not resolve these gaps in the submitted manuscript.

The MNIST experiment relies on substantial objective-specific supervision. Section S.3.4 trains a classifier on 440,000 labeled three-digit images and reports 96.9% held-out accuracy before constructing the optimization embeddings. Although the image splits are separated, this representation already contains extensive information about the optimization target. A baseline that directly ranks candidates using the pretrained classifier is needed to establish the additional value of Bayesian optimization.

Evidence for generality and practical scalability is limited. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions. No timing or memory measurements accompany dense graph construction and 1,000 acquisition-optimizer restarts, and the pool-subsampling study uses small synthetic pools. Consequently, the practical cost of the method on the much larger application pools remains difficult to assess.

Additional correctable issues affect technical clarity: the elementwise transition-probability definition implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W and Eq. (6) uses its transpose, leaving the intended propagation operator ambiguous. Equation (9) omits the Gaussian normalization factor. The plots also do not define their shaded uncertainty bands, limiting assessment of the reliability of smaller performance differences.
